title: Optogenetics
text:
CHAPTER 12  NEW TOOLS

12_01  OPTOGENETICS: CONTROLLING NEURONS WITH LIGHT

For most of the history told in this book, neuroscientists could do one of two things to a living brain. They could watch it, with electrodes, scalp recordings or scanners, or they could break it, with lesions, drugs or electrical stimulation. Watching tells you what correlates with what. Breaking tells you what is necessary, but crudely: a lesion destroys everything in a region, and an electrode stimulating tissue activates every axon and cell body near its tip, regardless of type. Imagine trying to debug a printed circuit board when your only tools are an oscilloscope probe and a soldering iron used as a hammer. You would learn a great deal, but you would never be sure which component did what.

Optogenetics changed this. It is the technique of making specific, genetically defined neurons sensitive to light, so that an experimenter can switch them on or off with millisecond precision while the animal behaves. For a mechatronics student, the cleanest description is that it gives neuroscience a set of addressable actuators. Instead of driving a whole region, you drive one cell class, defined by the genes it expresses, with a signal whose timing you control as precisely as a microcontroller controls a PWM output.

A WISH FROM FRANCIS CRICK

The idea that light might be the ideal control signal was articulated before anyone had the means to do it. Francis Crick, who turned to neuroscience in the later part of his career, wrote in the late 1990s that one of the great needs of the field was a method to turn on or off all neurons of one type in a region while leaving others unaffected, and he speculated that light might be suitable, because it can be delivered rapidly and precisely. He did not know how to make neurons respond to light. The answer came from an unexpected place: single-celled algae and salt-loving microbes.

MICROBIAL OPSINS

Animal eyes use opsins, proteins that bind a light-absorbing molecule called retinal. When retinal absorbs a photon it changes shape, the opsin changes conformation, and in our photoreceptors this triggers a G-protein cascade (Chapter 8). That cascade is slow and requires a lot of cellular machinery. Microbes evolved a different, simpler family of opsins in which the protein itself is the effector: it is an ion pump or ion channel that is directly opened or driven by light.

Three classes matter most.

1. Bacteriorhodopsin, studied since the 1970s in the archaeon Halobacterium salinarum by Dieter Oesterhelt and Walther Stoeckenius, is a light-driven proton pump. Absorbing a photon moves a proton out of the cell.

2. Halorhodopsin, from the same group of organisms, is a light-driven chloride pump that moves chloride ions into the cell.

3. Channelrhodopsins, discovered in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, are light-gated cation channels. The alga uses them to steer toward light. Georg Nagel, Peter Hegemann, Ernst Bamberg and colleagues characterised channelrhodopsin-1 in 2002 and channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in 2003, showing that ChR2 expressed in frog oocytes and mammalian cells produced a light-gated inward current, and suggesting it could be used to depolarise cells.

For an electrophysiologist the meaning was immediate. A cation channel that opens under blue light, admitting mostly sodium (and some protons, potassium and calcium), will depolarise a neuron. If the depolarisation is large enough, the cell fires an action potential. A chloride pump driven by yellow light will hyperpolarise a neuron and silence it.

THE 2005 PAPER

In 2005 Edward Boyden, Feng Zhang, Ernst Bamberg, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth published "Millisecond-timescale, genetically targeted optical control of neural activity" in Nature Neuroscience. They delivered the ChR2 gene into cultured hippocampal neurons using a viral vector and showed that brief pulses of blue light reliably evoked single spikes, and that trains of pulses could drive spike trains with the timing set by the light. Other groups reported related results at around the same time, which is common when a technique's time has come. In 2007 Zhang, Boyden, Deisseroth and colleagues showed in Nature that halorhodopsin from Natronomonas pharaonis (NpHR), driven by yellow light, could silence neurons, and that ChR2 and NpHR could be combined in the same cell for bidirectional control with two colours.

Why did this work so well? Let us reason with the membrane equations from Chapter 5. The membrane is modelled as a capacitor C_m in parallel with conductances. Adding an opsin adds one more term:

  C_m dV/dt = - g_L (V - E_L) - g_Na m^3 h (V - E_Na) - g_K n^4 (V - E_K) - g_ChR(t) (V - E_ChR) + I_ext

Here g_ChR(t) is the light-dependent conductance of channelrhodopsin, and E_ChR is its reversal potential, close to 0 mV because the channel passes several cations. At rest, V is around -65 mV, so (V - E_ChR) is strongly negative and the opsin current is inward, depolarising the cell. If light raises g_ChR enough, V crosses the threshold region where the sodium activation m runs away, and the Hodgkin-Huxley machinery produces a spike. The light does not need to produce the spike itself; it only needs to push the cell over its own threshold. That is why a channel with modest single-channel conductance (ChR2's is very small, much smaller than a typical voltage-gated sodium channel) works if enough copies are expressed.

A pump is different. NpHR moves one chloride ion per photocycle, independent of the membrane potential's driving force in the simple channel sense, so it produces a hyperpolarising current roughly proportional to light intensity. It needs relatively high light power and continuous illumination. Later inhibitory tools included archaerhodopsin (Arch), a proton pump reported by Chow, Boyden and colleagues in 2010, and engineered or natural anion-conducting channelrhodopsins, which silence neurons by clamping the membrane near the chloride reversal potential (shunting inhibition, as described in Chapter 6).

KINETICS: THE TIME CONSTANTS THAT MATTER

Each opsin has a photocycle: absorption, conformational change, channel opening, then closing and recovery. For wild-type ChR2 the channel closes with a time constant on the order of 10 milliseconds after light offset, which limits how fast it can drive spikes; at high frequencies the conductance does not fully turn off between pulses, and the neuron may fire extra spikes or fail. Engineers responded as engineers do, by mutating the protein. Variants with faster closing (for example ChETA, from Gunaydin, Deisseroth and colleagues) allow higher-frequency driving. Variants with very slow closing, called step-function opsins, stay open for seconds to minutes after a brief pulse and can be closed by a second colour, turning the opsin into a bistable switch rather than a pulse generator. Red-shifted channelrhodopsins such as Chrimson, reported by Klapoetke, Boyden and colleagues in 2014, respond to longer wavelengths, which scatter less in tissue and allow independent control of two populations with two colours.

The design space looks familiar to anyone who has chosen a MOSFET: switching speed, on-resistance (conductance), gate sensitivity (light power needed), spectral response, and leakage. Opsin engineering is device engineering at the molecular scale.

GETTING THE GENE INTO THE RIGHT CELLS

The "genetic" in optogenetics is the half that makes the technique precise. The opsin gene is placed after a promoter, a stretch of DNA that controls where the gene is expressed. Two strategies dominate.

Promoter-based targeting puts the opsin under a promoter that is active mostly in one cell type, for example CaMKIIa for many excitatory pyramidal neurons in the forebrain. This is simple but limited, because promoters that fit inside a viral vector are often not very specific.

Cre-lox targeting is more powerful. Thousands of transgenic mouse lines exist in which the bacteriophage enzyme Cre recombinase is expressed only in a defined cell type: dopamine neurons, parvalbumin-positive interneurons, somatostatin interneurons, and so on. The experimenter injects an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying an opsin gene that is inverted and flanked by lox sites (a so-called double-floxed inverted open reading frame, DIO). Only in cells that contain Cre does the gene get flipped into the correct orientation and expressed. The result is a logical AND: opsin expression occurs only where the virus was injected AND the cell expresses Cre. Intersectional strategies with two recombinases (Cre and Flp) extend this to AND gates of two genetic markers.

Light is delivered through an implanted optical fibre a few hundred micrometres in diameter, connected to a laser or LED, or for cortical surfaces through a cranial window. Because tissue scatters and absorbs light, the volume illuminated is limited, which is both a constraint and a form of spatial targeting. Light also heats tissue; careful experiments include controls with light but no opsin to rule out heating artefacts.

WHAT OPTOGENETICS REVEALED

The technique turned many correlational claims into causal tests. A few examples, chosen because they connect to earlier chapters:

Dopamine and reward. Chapter 6 described dopamine neurons as signalling reward prediction error. In 2009 Tsai, Deisseroth and colleagues reported in Science that phasic (burst-like) optogenetic stimulation of dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area was sufficient to produce a conditioned place preference in mice: animals came to prefer the place where they had received the stimulation. Later studies showed that optogenetically timed dopamine activity could act like a prediction error signal in learning tasks. For reinforcement learning, this is close to a direct test of the claim that the brain broadcasts a scalar teaching signal.

Memory engrams. In 2012 Liu, Ramirez, Tonegawa and colleagues reported in Nature that hippocampal dentate gyrus cells active during fear conditioning could be tagged, using an activity-dependent promoter linked to ChR2, and that reactivating those cells with light later caused mice to freeze in a different context. This made Semon's old idea of an "engram" (Chapter 9) experimentally tractable: a sparse set of cells whose reactivation is sufficient to evoke a memory-related behaviour.

Interneurons and gamma rhythms. Studies in 2009 from the Moore and Tsai laboratories (Cardin and colleagues) and from Sohal, Deisseroth and colleagues used optogenetics to drive parvalbumin-positive interneurons and showed their role in generating gamma-band oscillations in cortex, linking cell types to the EEG rhythms of Chapter 10.

Circuits for behaviour. Optogenetic activation or silencing of specific projections, not just cell bodies, became routine: illuminating axon terminals in a target region activates only the pathway from one area to another. This makes it possible to ask which connection, out of the many leaving a region, carries the signal needed for a behaviour.

LIMITATIONS AND CAUTIONS

Optogenetics is powerful but not magic, and honest use requires knowing its failure modes.

Synchrony artefacts. Light pulses drive all expressing cells at once, producing synchronous activity that rarely occurs naturally. A behaviour evoked this way shows what the circuit can do, not necessarily what it normally does.

Network compensation. Silencing a region acutely can produce deficits that disappear when the same region is lesioned permanently, because the rest of the network adapts. Otchy, Olveczky and colleagues reported in 2015 that acute and chronic manipulations of the same circuit could give different behavioural outcomes. The lesson is that "necessary" depends on timescale.

Off-target effects. Inhibiting axon terminals with pumps can paradoxically increase release in some conditions, and prolonged pumping of chloride shifts the chloride reversal potential. Heat from light can change firing on its own.

Expression variability. Different cells express different amounts of opsin, so the same light pulse does not produce the same effect in every cell.

These are not reasons to dismiss the technique; they are reasons to design controls, exactly as a careful engineer characterises an actuator before trusting a closed-loop system built on it.

READING AND WRITING TOGETHER

A natural extension combines optogenetic stimulation with optical recording, using the calcium and voltage indicators described in the next section. With two-photon holographic stimulation, light can be targeted to individual chosen cells in a field of view, sometimes tens of cells at once, while their neighbours are imaged. This is "all-optical" electrophysiology. Experiments in mouse visual cortex have used it to activate small ensembles of neurons and observe effects on perception-like behaviour, and to measure how stimulating one cell influences others, mapping functional connectivity directly.

CLINICAL STEPS

Because the opsin must be delivered by gene therapy, clinical use is harder than in mice. The most advanced application is in the retina, which is optically accessible. In 2021 Sahel and colleagues reported in Nature Medicine a patient with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys photoreceptors, who was treated with a viral vector expressing a red-shifted channelrhodopsin (ChrimsonR) in retinal ganglion cells and used light-stimulating goggles; the patient partially recovered the ability to locate and count some objects. It was a single-patient report, and the authors were careful about its scope, but it showed that optogenetics can operate in a human nervous system.

In 2021 the Lasker Basic Medical Research Award was given to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Dieter Oesterhelt for the discovery of light-sensitive microbial proteins and their use in optogenetics, reflecting how the field joined basic microbiology with neuroscience.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Interventions versus observations. Machine learning researchers know the difference between correlation and causation from causal inference: observational data can be explained by many causal graphs, but interventions (Judea Pearl's do-operator) distinguish them. Before optogenetics, most neural data was observational. Optogenetics is a do-operator for neurons: do(cell type X = active). That is why it transformed the logic of experiments. The analogy runs both ways. Interpretability research on neural networks moved from looking at activations (observational) to ablating, patching and steering activations (interventional). "Activation patching" and "causal tracing" in transformers, in which the activation of one component is replaced by that from another input to see what changes downstream, are conceptually optogenetic experiments on artificial networks. The difference is that in a model you can intervene on every unit perfectly and repeatably, which is exactly what neuroscientists wish they could do.

2. Cell types as architectural priors. Optogenetics showed that genetically defined cell types play distinct computational roles: parvalbumin interneurons for fast perisomatic inhibition and gamma rhythms, somatostatin interneurons for dendritic inhibition, VIP interneurons for disinhibition. Standard deep networks have one unit type with one nonlinearity. Some researchers argue that diverse, typed units with structured connectivity, like the canonical cortical microcircuit, may be useful inductive biases, for example in gating mechanisms. Gated units in LSTMs and multiplicative gating in modern architectures are loose functional analogues of inhibitory gating, though the correspondence is metaphorical rather than exact.

3. Ablations need care in both fields. The finding that acute silencing and chronic lesions can disagree has a direct AI parallel: zero-ablating a component of a trained network can show a large effect, while retraining after removing it may show the network compensates. Conversely, networks contain redundancy that hides a component's role under single ablations; researchers have described "self-repair" effects in language models where downstream layers partially compensate for ablated attention heads. Both neuroscientists and interpretability researchers have learned that "removing X changes Y" is a statement about the system under a specific intervention, not a complete description of X's function.

4. Closed-loop control. Optogenetics combined with real-time recording allows closed-loop experiments, where light is triggered by detected neural events, such as a seizure onset or a specific oscillation phase. This is control engineering on biological plant dynamics, and it connects to the brain-computer interfaces of Chapter 14 and to reinforcement learning agents that learn stimulation policies.

SUMMARY

Optogenetics put light-gated microbial channels and pumps into chosen neurons, giving millisecond, cell-type-specific control. Its biophysics is a simple extra conductance term in the membrane equation; its precision comes from genetics (promoters, Cre-lox, viral vectors); its scientific value comes from turning correlations into interventions. Its limits, including synchrony, compensation and expression variability, are instructive for anyone who intervenes on a complex network, whether made of cells or of matrices.
